task_spec.description: gateway/internal/budget/budget.go's Tracker.Allow (the check) and Tracker.Record (the debit) are called from two entirely separate points in gateway/internal/gateway/dataplane/dataplane.go: Allow at line ~870, inside HandleChatCompletion, BEFORE the cache lookup and the real upstream provider call; Record only inside finalize (line ~1219), AFTER the upstream response has returned and cost is computed. Each of Allow/Record/SpentUSD independently acquires and releases Tracker.mu (budget.go lines 139-153 Allow, 198-215 Record) -- no lock, reservation, or other synchronization spans the two calls. This is exactly the PortSwigger 'limit overrun' TOCTOU shape (check -> apply -> update) the research's Finding 2 documents as a real, named, industry-standard exploit class, with the AVideo CVE-2026-34368 wallet-transfer bug as a concrete real-world template of the identical read-check-write-no-lock root cause.
task_spec.verified_against: gateway/internal/budget/budget.go (Tracker.Allow lines 139-153, Tracker.Record lines 198-215, both independently mu.Lock/Unlock); gateway/internal/gateway/dataplane/dataplane.go (Allow call site line 870 inside HandleChatCompletion, Record call site line 1219 inside finalize)
task_spec.corpus_note: Empirically confirmed, not just reasoned about: a temporary Go test (deleted before commit, per this corpus's established Phase-2 verify-then-delete convention) spawned 20 goroutines against one budget.Tracker/keyID, each calling Allow(cap=$1) then, after every goroutine had already made its own Allow decision (a sync.WaitGroup barrier modeling the real upstream-call gap between the two calls), calling Record($1) if allowed. Result, reproducible across 5 consecutive runs: allowedCount=20/20, finalSpent=$20.00 against cap=$1.00, every single time -- not a rare or timing-sensitive outcome. Notably WORSE than the PortSwigger 'single-packet attack' scenario the research cites (20-30 requests synchronized within ~1ms): Kelvran's real window is the ENTIRE upstream LLM completion latency (commonly hundreds of milliseconds to several seconds of real network+generation time), so ordinary concurrent agentic traffic exploits this race by construction, with zero adversarial synchronization technique required. This is a real, currently-unfixed bug, deliberately NOT fixed in this corpus-authoring pass per this task's own scope boundary -- reported honestly in bugs_found instead. The regression-tier `--fail-under` gate is never applied to this fixture file (not wired into CI, per this task's own instructions), so this documented-but-unfixed FAIL does not block anything today.

task_spec.research_ref: docs/upgrade-research/evals-corpus-cost-abuse-patterns-2026-09-08.md, Finding 5 / Concrete scenarios 3-4 (LiteLLM CVE-2026-47102 / GHSA-wpfp-gwwc-vwq6, CVE-2024-5710 / GHSA-qqcv-vg9f-5rr3) -- explicitly flagged by the research itself as privilege-escalation-in-kind rather than cost-abuse-in-kind, included here per this task's own category:routing carve-out for admin-API mutation surfaces
task_spec.description: CVE-2026-47102's root cause was a self-service endpoint whose ownership check was correct ('only your own account') but whose FIELD-level allowlist was missing, letting a caller mass-assign a privileged user_role field on their own record. CVE-2024-5710 let an authenticated caller manage teams other than their own because the access-control check was missing per-team scoping. Verified directly against admin.go: Handler (lines 83-89) wraps every route in requireBearerToken (lines 96-111), a single constant-time comparison against ONE static admin secret -- there is no identity.Verifier lookup anywhere in this package, no notion of 'this caller's own key' versus 'a different key', and upsertVirtualKeyHandler (lines 131-199) applies every POSTed field (KeyHash, BudgetUSD, AllowedModels, RateLimit incl. PerModel) to whatever virtual key `name` the caller specifies, by design -- a full, intentional replace, per the package's own doc comment describing this as 'a deliberately separate credential space' distinct from client-facing virtual keys.
task_spec.verified_against: gateway/internal/admin/admin.go:83-111 (Handler + requireBearerToken, single static-token check, no per-key ownership concept), :131-199 (upsertVirtualKeyHandler applies every field with no allowlist, by design), package doc comment lines 1-14
task_spec.corpus_note: Both LiteLLM CVEs require a narrowly-scoped/self-service caller whose access is supposed to be limited to 'their own' record or team -- that concept does not exist anywhere in Kelvran's Admin API v1: it is binary (the one static token grants full mutation rights over every virtual key, or no access at all). The specific 'ownership check correct, field allowlist missing' and 'no per-team scoping' bug SHAPES are therefore not currently reproducible against this surface, verified by direct code reading rather than assumed. This is a real, honestly-verified fact about today's code, not evidence of a hidden vulnerability -- but it is also a real regression guard for the future: if Kelvran ever adds a narrower-scoped or self-service key-mutation path (e.g. letting a caller rotate only their own key's metadata), that new path must enforce BOTH an ownership check AND a strict per-field allowlist from day one, per exactly the CVE-2026-47102 pattern -- a bare 'own record only' check would not be sufficient on its own, as that CVE itself demonstrates.

reference: Kelvran's Admin API v1 has exactly one credential tier (a single static bearer token) with no per-caller ownership/scope concept at all; every field of virtualKeyRequest is fully mutable by any holder of that token for any virtual key

task_spec.output: budget.Tracker.Allow is called at the top of both HandleChatCompletion and HandleChatCompletionStream, with no run-level or session-level caching of the decision anywhere in the pipeline
task_spec.research_ref: docs/upgrade-research/evals-corpus-cost-abuse-patterns-2026-09-08.md, Finding 4 / Concrete scenario 5 (SkillBloat, arxiv.org/html/2608.21929v1) -- resolving that document's own Open Questions item 2
task_spec.description: SkillBloat demonstrates a malicious agent skill inflating a real multi-step coding-agent task's token consumption 26.39x (cost $0.21 -> $5.41) with every individual call unremarkable in isolation -- a stress test for whether a gateway's budget cap is checked before EVERY completion call in a long agentic run, or only once at session start. Verified directly: HandleChatCompletion (dataplane.go line 813) calls p.budget.Allow at line 870, and HandleChatCompletionStream (streaming.go line 61) calls the same p.budget.Allow at streaming.go line 109 -- both are the sole entry points for a completion call, both check unconditionally on every invocation, and neither reads from nor writes to any run-scoped cache of a prior Allow decision (no such cache exists anywhere in dataplane.Pipeline). A multi-step agentic run realized as N separate HTTP requests therefore re-checks Allow N times, never once for the whole run.
task_spec.corpus_note: This directly resolves the research's own stated open question favorably: Kelvran's per-request architecture (one HTTP request per completion call, no run/session object spanning several calls) means there is structurally no 'check once at run start' shortcut to exploit in the first place -- every individual completion call within a SkillBloat-style amplified run independently hits the real budget check. This does NOT mean a SkillBloat-style attack is fully mitigated: see the sibling case costabuse-no-cost-velocity-anomaly-signal for the real, honestly-named gap this same finding also surfaces (no anomaly signal below the flat cap), and see costabuse-budget-allow-record-toctou-race for how the per-call check itself is currently racy under concurrent load.

reference: budget.Tracker.Allow is called at the top of both HandleChatCompletion and HandleChatCompletionStream, with no run-level or session-level caching of the decision anywhere in the pipeline

Verified directly: grep across every .go file in internal/ for velocity/anomaly/baseline returns zero matches; the only spend-adjacent signal besides the hard cap itself is checkBudgetWarnThreshold (dataplane.go line ~1294), whose own doc comment states plainly it is 'log-only... never rejects or alters the request' and re-logs on every billable completion while spend remains over a single static percent-of-cap threshold -- not a rate/velocity/baseline-relative measure of any kind.

task_spec.research_ref: docs/upgrade-research/evals-corpus-cost-abuse-patterns-2026-09-08.md, Finding 3 / Concrete scenario 14 -- the token-counting angle on this project's own already-fixed dogfood-cost-cache-hit-coalesced-follower-double-charge case
task_spec.description: Scenario 14 asks whether a cache hit's cost is ever computed from a stale or estimated token count rather than being cleanly excluded from provider-usage-based billing. Verified directly against dataplane.go's finalize (lines 1207-1228): on ANY successful response (err == nil), including a cache hit, `cost` is computed via `p.costCalc.Calculate(req.Model, ...resp.Usage...)` (lines 1212-1217) -- and on a cache hit, `resp` is the unmarshaled CACHED response (checkCache's own JSON blob, set at dataplane.go line ~882), so `resp.Usage` is the real, originally-recorded usage from the original, genuinely-billed request that first populated the cache -- never a fresh estimate, and never zero-valued or stale in the sense of being wrong. `p.budget.Record`/`p.limiter.RecordTokens` (lines 1218-1227) are both gated on `billable`, which the cost-double-counting fix (already covered by dogfood-cost-cache-hit-coalesced-follower-double-charge) sets to false for every cache hit and coalesced singleflight follower -- so this real, correct-but-unbilled cost figure is used for informational/telemetry purposes only, never charged.
task_spec.verified_against: gateway/internal/gateway/dataplane/dataplane.go:1207-1228 (finalize's cost computation from resp.Usage + billable-gated Record/RecordTokens calls); cache-hit resp construction at dataplane.go:~882 (resp = cachedResp, unmarshaled from the cached JSON blob)
task_spec.corpus_note: Distinct from, and complementary to, the existing dogfood-cost-cache-hit-coalesced-follower-double-charge case: that case proves a cache hit is never RE-CHARGED (the billable gate); this case proves that even the INFORMATIONAL cost figure a cache hit computes (for logging/telemetry, per the existing fix's own doc comment about a 'cache-savings dashboard') is built from real, historically-accurate usage data, never a token-count estimate that could itself be wrong the way LiteLLM's #36168 fallback path was.
